lessonTitle: Reasoning in Complex Cases: Synthesis, Bayes and Cognitive Bias

blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman has been seen by rheumatology for 'joint pain', by dermatology for a facial rash, by the chest clinic for pleuritic pain and by her GP for 'a bit of protein in the urine'. Four specialists each solved the part they were shown; nobody asked whether one disease could explain all four.

blocks.markdown: **Synthesis across systems.** Complex cases fail when each system is examined in isolation. Reasoning begins by writing down every abnormal finding, grouping them by system, and then asking which **single process** could produce the most findings with the fewest assumptions. This is parsimony (Occam's razor). The counter-principle is that patients, especially older ones with many conditions, can have several unrelated problems, so after proposing a unifying diagnosis you must check what it does **not** explain.

blocks.title: Pre-test probability and likelihood ratio
blocks.text: The pre-test probability is the chance of the disease before the test result, estimated from the history, examination and prevalence in this setting. A likelihood ratio (LR) states how much a result multiplies the odds of disease: LR+ for a positive result, LR- for a negative result.

blocks.caption: Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased people who test positive; specificity is the proportion of non-diseased people who test negative.
Bayes' theorem in odds form. Convert probability to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, then convert back.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: updating a probability with a test result
blocks.prompt: A patient has a pre-test probability of 25% for a disease. A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 85%. Find the post-test probability after a positive result and after a negative result.

steps.text: Compute the likelihood ratios: LR+ = 0.90 / (1 - 0.85) = 6.0 and LR- = (1 - 0.90) / 0.85 = 0.118.
Convert the pre-test probability to odds: 0.25 / 0.75 = 0.333 (that is 1 to 3).
Positive result: post-test odds = 0.333 x 6 = 2.0, so the probability is 2.0 / 3.0 = 66.7%. The test moved the probability substantially but does not make it certain.

Negative result: post-test odds = 0.333 x 0.118 = 0.0392, so the probability is 0.0392 / 1.0392 = 3.8%. A negative result lowers, but does not abolish, the chance. Whether 3.8% is acceptable depends on how dangerous it is to miss the disease.

blocks.answer: Positive: about 67%. Negative: about 3.8%. The same test gives different post-test probabilities depending on the starting probability, which is why the pre-test estimate matters.

rows: Anchoring
Fixing on the first impression despite new data
Persisting with 'anxiety' despite abnormal results
Re-state the differential after each new result
Premature closure
Stopping the search once one explanation is found
Accepting 'urinary infection' for confusion without checking more
Ask 'what else could this be?' before finishing
Confirmation bias
Seeking or valuing evidence that supports the favoured diagnosis
Ordering only tests that can confirm
Seek disconfirming data deliberately
Availability
Over-estimating what is easy to recall
Suspecting a recently missed rare diagnosis in everyone
Use base rates and explicit probabilities
Diagnostic momentum
A label gains weight as it is handed on
'Known alcoholic' carried through successive notes
Re-take the history; treat inherited labels as hypotheses
Framing
Wording of a presentation steers the conclusion
'Drunk and fell' versus 'collapsed'
Reframe neutrally and restate the findings
blocks.caption: Common cognitive biases in diagnosis and a debiasing strategy for each.

blocks.markdown: **Why bias happens and what reduces it.** Fast, pattern-based thinking (System 1) is usually efficient but fails under fatigue, interruption and time pressure; slow analytical reasoning (System 2) is effortful. You cannot remove bias by willpower, so build habits that trigger deliberate review: a diagnostic time-out for any patient who is not improving, a short list of dangerous alternatives that must be actively excluded, requesting a second opinion, and recording your estimated probability so that you can learn from the outcome. Seeking feedback on cases where you were wrong improves calibration.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: a unifying diagnosis from four systems
blocks.prompt: A 34-year-old woman has symmetrical small-joint pain and morning stiffness for 3 months, a facial rash across the cheeks and nose that worsens in sunlight, pleuritic chest pain, urine dipstick showing protein 2+ and blood 1+, mild anaemia and a low platelet count. Propose a unifying diagnosis and plan.

steps.text: List by system: musculoskeletal (symmetrical inflammatory arthritis), skin (photosensitive malar rash), serosal (pleuritic pain suggesting pleurisy), renal (proteinuria and haematuria suggesting glomerular involvement), haematological (anaemia, thrombocytopenia).

Look for one process: a systemic autoimmune disease with immune-complex involvement across skin, joints, serosa, kidney and blood. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) explains all findings. Alternatives to hold on the list: drug-induced lupus, other connective-tissue disease, vasculitis, and infection or malignancy mimics.

Check what the unifying diagnosis does not explain, and choose discriminating tests. ANA is sensitive for SLE but not specific, so a positive result alone has a modest effect on probability; anti-dsDNA antibodies and low complement are more specific and also relate to disease activity. Urine microscopy, a urine protein quantification and renal function are needed because kidney involvement changes management.

Plan: urgent referral to rheumatology and nephrology, tissue diagnosis (renal biopsy) if indicated, medicines and monitoring chosen by specialists; classification criteria and treatment options should be taken from current EULAR/ACR and BNF sources rather than from memory.

blocks.answer: A unifying diagnosis of probable SLE with renal involvement, confirmed through targeted serology and urine tests, with renal and rheumatology referral. The method matters more than the label: group, unify, test what the diagnosis does not explain.

items: Write the full list of abnormal findings before choosing a diagnosis.
Ask which single diagnosis explains most findings, then ask what it fails to explain.
State a pre-test probability before ordering a test, and state how the result would change management.
Name the dangerous alternative that must be excluded and the test that does it.
Run a diagnostic time-out when the patient is not improving.

blocks.title: Tests do not give diagnoses
blocks.text: A positive result from a highly specific test in a very low-risk population is more likely to be a false positive than a true one. Always interpret a result against the pre-test probability, not alone.

points: Group findings by system, then look for one process that explains most of them, and check what it leaves unexplained.
Convert probability to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, and convert back; the same result affects a high and a low pre-test probability very differently.
Common biases (anchoring, premature closure, confirmation, availability, diagnostic momentum, framing) are managed by deliberate habits such as time-outs and explicit alternatives.
Treatments and diagnostic criteria must be taken from current NICE, BNF and specialty guidance rather than recalled.

questions.stem: A registrar remarks that last week a patient with 'indigestion' proved to have a ruptured aortic aneurysm, and now orders a CT angiogram for every patient with epigastric discomfort. Which cognitive bias best explains this behaviour?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a vivid, recent case makes the diagnosis seem more probable than its true base rate.
distractorRationale.b: Anchoring means holding on to a first impression despite new data, which is not described.
distractorRationale.c: Momentum describes a label passed down successive clinicians.
distractorRationale.d: Confirmation bias is selective seeking of supporting data after a diagnosis is chosen.

questions.explanation: Availability bias is the overestimate of the probability of a diagnosis because it is easy to recall. The remedy is to apply base rates and an explicit probability estimate, not to order a high-risk test for everyone.

questions.stem: A patient is found to have a fractured wrist on X-ray after a fall, and the team stops looking. Later a subdural haematoma is found; the patient had a head strike and drowsiness. Which bias is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the search was ended once one abnormality had been found.
distractorRationale.b: No recent memorable case is described.
distractorRationale.c: Not described: nothing about how the case was worded.
distractorRationale.d: No test was falsely reassuring; the search simply stopped.

questions.explanation: Stopping after the first plausible finding is premature closure or search satisficing. The countermeasure is to ask what else could be present, especially for injuries with a plausible mechanism for several problems.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has cough, haemoptysis and weight loss for 2 months, and a sodium of 118 mmol/L with low serum osmolality, concentrated urine and no oedema or hypovolaemia. Which single explanation best unifies these findings?

options.text: A lung tumour causing the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Primary polydipsia with an unrelated chest infection

questions.correctOptionText: A lung tumour causing the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a lung malignancy explains haemoptysis and weight loss, and ectopic ADH production explains hyponatraemia with concentrated urine in a euvolaemic patient.
distractorRationale.b: Primary polydipsia would give dilute urine, not concentrated urine.
distractorRationale.c: Adrenal insufficiency usually gives hypovolaemia and hyperkalaemia; the findings do not fit.
distractorRationale.d: Heart failure causes hyponatraemia with oedema and hypervolaemia, which are absent.

questions.explanation: The unifying diagnosis explains both the respiratory features and the metabolic derangement with one process. Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low osmolality and concentrated urine points to SIADH, and a lung tumour is a classic cause; confirm with tests and imaging.

questions.stem: A clinician estimates the pre-test probability of a disease at 10%. A test has a positive likelihood ratio of 8 and gives a positive result. Calculate the post-test probability as a percentage to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Pre-test odds = 0.10 / 0.90 = 0.111. Post-test odds = 0.111 x 8 = 0.889, so probability = 0.889 / 1.889 = 47.1%. A positive test raised the probability from 10% to about 47%, which still leaves it below 50%, so further confirmation may be needed.

questions.stem: A screening test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. It is applied to 10,000 people in a population where the disease prevalence is 2%. Calculate the positive predictive value as a percentage to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Diseased people: 200 of whom 180 test positive (true positives). Non-diseased: 9,800 of whom 5% (490) test positive (false positives). PPV = 180 / (180 + 490) = 26.9%. Even with good sensitivity and specificity, low prevalence means most positives are false positives.

questions.stem: The same test is positive in two patients: one in a low-risk population and one in a high-risk population. Why do their positive predictive values differ?

options.text: Because the pre-test probability (prevalence) is different in the two groups
Because the test's sensitivity changes with the patient's risk
Because positive tests are always more accurate in low-risk patients
Because specificity depends on the clinician's experience

questions.correctOptionText: Because the pre-test probability (prevalence) is different in the two groups

distractorRationale.a: Correct: predictive value depends on the pre-test probability as well as the test characteristics.
distractorRationale.b: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test, not of the patient's risk.
distractorRationale.c: The reverse is true: low prevalence gives lower PPV.
distractorRationale.d: Specificity is not determined by who orders the test.

questions.explanation: Positive predictive value rises with prevalence. A positive test in a high-risk patient is more likely to be a true positive because the starting probability is higher.

questions.stem: A positive result from a test with very high specificity proves the disease is present, whatever the pre-test probability.
questions.explanation: Even a very specific test produces false positives, and when the pre-test probability is very low those false positives can outnumber the true positives. Interpretation always needs the pre-test probability.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has had 3 weeks of fever and night sweats, a new regurgitant murmur, splinter haemorrhages, microscopic haematuria and low back pain. Which unifying diagnosis best explains all findings?

options.text: Infective endocarditis with embolic or immune-complex phenomena and possible spinal infection
Simple mechanical back pain with coincidental urinary infection

questions.correctOptionText: Infective endocarditis with embolic or immune-complex phenomena and possible spinal infection

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fever with a new regurgitant murmur, vascular phenomena, haematuria and back pain (possible discitis) fit one process.
distractorRationale.b: Does not explain the murmur, the vascular phenomena or the haematuria.
distractorRationale.c: Treats each finding as separate and does not explain the murmur or splinter haemorrhages.
distractorRationale.d: Gout does not explain fever, murmur or splinter haemorrhages.

questions.explanation: A new murmur with fever is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise. Splinter haemorrhages and haematuria reflect embolic or immune-complex disease, and back pain can reflect spinal infection; confirm with blood cultures and echocardiography per current guidance.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man attends the emergency department with central chest pain. At triage he is labelled 'anxious, probably musculoskeletal' and no ECG is recorded. The next clinician reads the label, does not take a new history, and discharges him with analgesia. He returns the next day with an ECG showing ST elevation. Identify the cognitive biases and explain how they could have been reduced.
markingGuide: Anchoring on the triage label of anxiety or musculoskeletal pain
Diagnostic momentum: the triage label was accepted and carried forward without a fresh history
Premature closure: the dangerous alternatives (acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism) were not actively excluded
Possible framing effect from the way the patient was described, and age-related low prior probability bias

Debiasing: take an independent history and examination, record an ECG promptly in anyone with chest pain, write a differential including must-not-miss diagnoses, use a diagnostic time-out and seek senior review before discharge
Treat inherited labels as hypotheses; document the reasoning and safety-net advice
questions.explanation: A good answer names the specific biases, links each to something in the vignette and proposes concrete counter-measures rather than general exhortations. Credit is given for explaining why each measure interrupts the bias.

questions.stem: A test for a disease has sensitivity 99% and specificity 90%. In 1,000 patients seen in primary care the disease prevalence is 1%. Using natural frequencies, explain what proportion of positive results are true positives and what this means for how the test should be used.
markingGuide: Ten diseased people, of whom about 9.9 test positive (true positives)
990 non-diseased people, of whom 10% (99) test positive (false positives)
PPV = 9.9 / (9.9 + 99) = about 9%, so roughly nine in ten positives are false positives
A high sensitivity gives a good negative predictive value but does not make a positive result reliable when prevalence is low
Implication: use the test selectively in patients with a raised pre-test probability or as a first step followed by a confirmatory test; interpret in context
questions.explanation: Natural frequencies show that prevalence drives predictive value. Even with 99% sensitivity, a low pre-test probability and imperfect specificity mean most positive results are false. Test choice should therefore follow the pre-test probability.
